explanation.headline: HIGH: a trailing vehicle closed on a slower vehicle ahead
bullets: car #38 and car #86 travel in the same direction; the trailing vehicle is closing on the one ahead.
At constant speed their footprints would meet in about 1.17s, inside the 2.0s look-ahead window.
Projected footprints overlap: 0.0px apart against a 48.0px combined footprint.
The pair was closing at 47px/s in image space.
Across the observed episode, the longest consecutive run at HIGH lasted 3 frames; a minimum consecutive run is required, so a single noisy frame cannot raise this warning.
explanation.caveat: Image-space pixels and constant-velocity projection; not a measured speed, distance, or collision probability.

- Source: Real traffic sample (real_traffic_demo): real_traffic_sample.mp4

- Real traffic footage: “Traffic Flow In The Highway” by Mike Bird (https://www.pexels.com/video/traffic-flow-in-the-highway-2103099/; Pexels License, https://www.pexels.com/license/). Bundled sample, not your upload.

- Footage analyzed: 00:15.0

## Crossing-distance illustration (assumptions, not measurements)

- Current crossing distance: 60 ft
- Hypothetical crossing distance: 40 ft
- Start-up time: 2 s

| Walker | Speed (ft/s) | Current (s) | Hypothetical (s) | Hypothetical vs current | Time in roadway |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Typical walking speed | 3.5 | 19.1 | 13.4 | 5.7 s shorter | 33.3% less time |
| Slower walking speed | 2.5 | 26.0 | 18.0 | 8.0 s shorter | 33.3% less time |

_Crossing times are arithmetic on the assumptions entered above (distance ÷ walking speed + start-up time). They illustrate time spent in the roadway; they are not a measured crash reduction or a prediction of safety outcomes._

**Any design change discussed here is a review hypothesis. It requires field measurement, local context, and qualified engineering review before any decision.**

## Follow-up observation checklist

- [ ] At flagged crossing-path moments, note who had right-of-way and whether sight lines were blocked (parked vehicles, vegetation, building corners). — _Crossing-path warnings were flagged in this footage._
- [ ] On the flagged approach, observe queues and sudden stops and note what triggered braking (pedestrian, turning vehicle, signal change). — _Same-direction following warnings were flagged in this footage._
- [ ] Observe turning movements across opposing traffic and the gaps drivers accept. — _Opposing or turning-path warnings were flagged in this footage._
- [ ] Ask whether the responsible agency has its own records for the flagged time; do not assume a crash occurred. — _A suspected-incident candidate was found and needs independent confirmation._
- [ ] Measure curb-to-curb crossing distance on each leg and record lane widths. — _Replaces the assumed distances above with field measurements._
- [ ] Record date, time, weather, lighting, and camera position for every observation. — _Makes repeated observations comparable._
- [ ] Repeat observation on several days, including peak and off-peak periods. — _One clip cannot show whether a pattern is typical._
- [ ] Check curb ramps, detectable warnings, pushbutton reach, and crossing signal timing. — _Accessibility gaps affect slower walkers most._
- [ ] Talk with people who use the intersection daily (residents, crossing guards, bus riders). — _Local experience explains context the camera cannot see._

## Boundaries

- No crash records, city data, or real incidents are used. Counts below come only from the active video's processed detections and this operator's reviews.
- Crossing times are arithmetic on the assumptions entered above (distance ÷ walking speed + start-up time). They illustrate time spent in the roadway; they are not a measured crash reduction or a prediction of safety outcomes.
- Any design change discussed here is a review hypothesis. It requires field measurement, local context, and qualified engineering review before any decision.
